whyCorrect: Read the sentence as a contrast: the blank has to name the opposite of a merit for this particular trade. The builders in question disliked the machine-made brick precisely because it was too uniform, and they kept paying more for the slower moulded work to avoid it. So the machine's regularity actually cost it business with them, which makes it a drawback — a liability.

whyWrong.A: Nothing about the regularity is unexplained or puzzling; the builders understood exactly what it was and objected to it.
whyWrong.B: A bargain would make the machine brick more attractive to these builders, but the passage says they paid extra to avoid it.
whyWrong.D: A necessity would mean the trade required the regularity, the reverse of the complaint described.

commonMistakes: Filling the blank with a word about price or value instead of tracking the “less a merit than” contrast, which demands a negative.
tips: When a blank sits after “less X than,” the word must be roughly the opposite of X.

whyCorrect: The reason clause does the work: the pattern “appears again at every level” because it was inlaid through the tile's whole thickness rather than painted on the surface. So wearing the tile down cannot remove the design — the blank needs a phrase meaning wear has no effect on it. “Powerless against” says exactly that.

whyWrong.A: “Invisible on” would mean the wear cannot be seen, but the passage is about whether the pattern survives, not whether the scuffing shows.
whyWrong.C: “Fatal to” reverses the logic: it says wear destroys the pattern, which the reason clause directly contradicts.
whyWrong.D: “Responsible for” would mean wear creates the pattern; the tiler created it by stamping and filling the clay.

tips: When a blank is followed by “because,” solve the because-clause first and make the blank agree with it.

whyCorrect: The bricks in the hacks are still soft, and the whole paragraph is about protecting them — gaps for air, a roof against rain and sun. The final sentence names what happens when that protection fails, and it ends “and lose the whole row,” so what rain does to the faces has to be ruinous. Here “raise” means it wrecks the surfaces of the bricks.

whyWrong.A: “Collect” is a real sense of raise (raise funds), but a shower does not gather the brick faces together.
whyWrong.B: “Lift up” is the most literal sense of raise, and it is what makes this choice tempting, but a rain shower does not elevate anything — and the sentence's consequence is loss, not movement.
whyWrong.C: “Cultivate” is the sense used of crops and livestock and has nothing to do with rain falling on unfired brick.

commonMistakes: Picking the most common dictionary meaning of the word instead of the one the sentence's consequence requires.

whyCorrect: The sentence before the blank tells you what to fill it with: the winter's freezing did work “the yard would otherwise have paid men to do.” Something that does the work of paid men is a worker. So the frost served the brickmaker as a labourer, breaking up the clay in place of a man with a hammer.

whyWrong.B: A customer buys the yard's output; frost consumed nothing and bought nothing.
whyWrong.C: A witness observes; the frost is described as acting on the clay, not watching.
whyWrong.D: A rival would compete with the brickmaker, but the frost saved him money rather than taking his trade.

tips: When the blank ends a sentence that begins with a summary of what something did, name the role that matches that action.

whyCorrect: The first sentence only reports that the holes exist and how they are arranged; the last sentence treats them as evidence an archaeologist can read. Nothing lets you jump from one to the other unless you know what made the holes. The underlined sentence supplies that missing link — the holes are the sockets of scaffold poles bedded in the rising wall — which is what makes the final inference about season and sequence possible.

whyWrong.A: It says nothing about spacing being wrong; it accepts the description and explains its cause.
whyWrong.B: The archaeologist's conclusions come afterward, in the sentence the underlined one makes possible.
whyWrong.D: It gives no specific wall or building; it explains the general cause of the holes.

tips: For function questions, ask what the following sentence could not claim if the underlined sentence were deleted.

whyCorrect: Track the three moves. The opening sentence sets out a problem: brick sizes varied locally and a bricklayer's rule stopped working twenty miles away. The middle sentence names the forces that ended the variation — a tax charged by the thousand and sale by the thousand at a distance. The last sentence gives the outcome, a size still in use. That is problem, cause of resolution, result.

whyWrong.A: No individual bricklayer is followed; he appears once as an illustration of the problem.
whyWrong.C: A rule is mentioned in passing, but the text is about brick size, not about a tool and its users.
whyWrong.D: Only one account is given, and the text endorses it rather than leaving two theories open.

tips: Structure questions are answered by the order of the moves, not by the topic.

whyCorrect: Both texts are looking at the same thing: the mass of overlaid lines scored into the tracing-floor plaster. Text 1 explains them as working drawings a mason made to full size so templates could be cut from them. Text 2 accepts that the lines are there but points to lines matching no window in the building and reads the whole floor as a teaching surface instead. Same evidence, competing explanation.

whyWrong.A: Text 1 never claims measurements are missing; it says the floor carried the shapes at their true size.
whyWrong.B: Text 2 relies on the lines existing — it counts them and notes which match built windows.
whyWrong.C: Only one floor is discussed; Text 2 does not move to a second building.

tips: When both texts describe one body of evidence, check whether the second reinterprets it rather than extending it.

whyCorrect: The question asks for the chief advantage of split lath, so find the property the text credits split lath with and the benefit that follows. Splitting follows the grain, so the fibres run unbroken end to end and the strip bends far before snapping; sawn lath cuts across the grain and breaks at every crossing. The last sentence confirms the payoff: sawn lath ceilings come down and split lath ones hold.

whyWrong.A: Being machinable from any part of the log is an advantage the text gives to sawn lath, not split.
whyWrong.B: Even width is also credited to sawn lath — the text says split lath never has it.
whyWrong.D: The text explicitly calls sawn lath the cheaper article.

commonMistakes: Grabbing an advantage stated in the passage without checking which of the two materials it belongs to.

whyCorrect: The main idea has to cover the whole passage, and the passage moves from a cause to a consequence. The cause: heat in a clamp is never the same in two parts of the heap, so middle bricks come out hard and dark while outer bricks come out pale and porous. The consequence, stated in the last sentence, is that the yard's first job is to sort the heap into qualities and price each one separately. That is the point of the text.

whyWrong.A: Cost is never compared with a kiln; the fuel is mentioned only as part of how a clamp is built.
whyWrong.C: The middle bricks are described as hard and dark — the good ones. It is the pale outer skin that a winter would ruin.
whyWrong.D: The clay daubing is one construction detail, and the text's whole argument is that the heat is not even.

tips: A main-idea choice that only restates one sentence is too narrow, even when that sentence is true.

whyCorrect: Lund's claim has two halves — countable products and uncountable ones — and each is paid differently. Only one quotation shows both at once: the setters are paid by time (eleven weeks at two shillings the week), which is how you pay for labour whose output cannot be counted, while William is paid by the piece (ninety mullion stones at threepence the stone), which is how you pay for output that can. The contrast inside a single entry is what illustrates the distinction.

whyWrong.A: This records materials delivered, not labour paid, so it shows neither side of the distinction.
whyWrong.B: The smith is paid a flat annual sum, which is one payment method with nothing to contrast it against.
whyWrong.D: This is half of the correct quotation. Piecework alone shows countable labour but not the time-paid labour Lund contrasts it with.

commonMistakes: Choosing a quotation that supports half an argument; a two-part claim needs a quotation that shows both parts.

whyCorrect: The passage tells you exactly what a lewis leaves behind: a small tapered slot cut in the top of the block, hidden once the block is bedded. A sling passed underneath leaves no such slot. So finding tapered slots in the upper beds of blocks taken out of this tower is the physical trace the method predicts, and it is what would support Raman.

whyWrong.A: Payments to masons show building work happened but say nothing about how blocks were lifted.
whyWrong.C: Heavier blocks might make a lewis useful, but weight alone does not show one was used — heavy blocks can be slung.
whyWrong.D: A lewis is iron, but stray iron of the right date could come from tools, fittings or anything else on site.

tips: For support questions, first name the observable trace the hypothesis predicts, then look for the choice that reports it.

whyCorrect: Read the table down: 38 mm allows 1.5 m, 50 mm allows 2.6 m, 63 mm allows 3.2 m. Thickness and permitted span rise together. Since transoms are what the boards rest on, a board that may span further needs supports less often, so thicker boards mean fewer transoms in a given length of scaffold.

whyWrong.B: This reverses the table — the thinnest board, 38 mm, has the shortest permitted span, 1.5 m.
whyWrong.C: 1.5 to 2.6 is not a doubling, and neither is 2.6 to 3.2. The spans increase but not by a fixed factor.
whyWrong.D: The table exists to show that thickness does change the permitted span, from 1.5 m to 3.2 m.

commonMistakes: Reading the trend correctly but then getting the consequence backwards — a longer permitted span means fewer supports, not more.

whyCorrect: The passage sets up a mismatch: the ruled lines are drawn to the proportions of handsome ashlar rather than to anything actually behind them, and the grooves are only millimetres deep while real stone blocks are as deep as they are broad. So the lines are decoration laid over the front, unconnected to the construction beneath. A viewer on the pavement therefore gets no information from them about how the wall is built.

whyWrong.B: Counting the courses only counts the scored rectangles, which the text says bear no relation to the wall behind, so no thickness follows.
whyWrong.C: The passage mentions a rough brick front in one instance but stresses that the lines tell you nothing about what is behind them.
whyWrong.D: The text says the opposite: the lines were run to handsome proportions rather than to the real joints.

tips: When a text insists two things do not correspond, the inference is almost always that one cannot be used to judge the other.

whyCorrect: The chain is: clay shrinks in drying and burning, so the mould is cut oversize by an allowance, and that allowance is fixed “by trial” for one particular clay. The last sentence stresses that the allowance belongs to the clay, not the mould. New ground means new clay, whose shrinkage is unknown until it has been tested, so the old moulds cannot be trusted until that measurement is made.

whyWrong.A: This assumes the allowance carries over, which is exactly what the sentence “belongs to the clay rather than to the mould” rules out.
whyWrong.C: Nothing suggests a new clay skips drying; all clay is said to give up water before burning.
whyWrong.D: Firing temperature is never discussed, and lowering it is not how the text says size is controlled.

commonMistakes: Treating “established by trial” as a one-time fact about brickmaking rather than a measurement that must be repeated for each clay.

whyCorrect: Everything before the blank is a complete sentence, and what follows names the tile that sentence has just built up to. A colon is the mark that introduces a name or explanation after a complete clause, so “purpose: a bonnet” is correct. The comma after “bonnet” then opens the participial phrase “moulded to sit astride the angle,” which describes it.

whyWrong.B: This runs “purpose” straight into “a bonnet” with no punctuation, leaving two noun phrases jammed together.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon must join two independent clauses. “A bonnet, moulded to sit astride the angle…” has no verb of its own, so it cannot stand after one.
whyWrong.D: The semicolon lands between “a bonnet” and the participle describing it, cutting the phrase off from the noun it modifies.

tips: Test a colon by covering the second half: if the first half stands alone as a sentence and the second half names or explains something in it, the colon is right.

whyCorrect: Strip the sentence to its bones: “The gutter… had a joint every few feet.” Everything between “gutter” and “had” is a restrictive relative clause telling you which gutter. No punctuation belongs between a subject and its verb, so the blank takes nothing at all.

whyWrong.A: A single comma here separates the subject from its verb, which Standard English does not allow.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon needs an independent clause on each side; “had a joint every few feet” has no subject.
whyWrong.D: A colon also requires a complete clause before it, and “The lead-lined gutter that used to be laid… at an inward angle” is only a subject.

commonMistakes: Adding a comma because the subject is long. Length never licenses a subject–verb comma.

whyCorrect: “A low bench of stone or heavy timber set at about waist height” is an appositive renaming “banker,” and it needs a comma to open it. The closing comma is already in the sentence, before “and drives.” The participle “set at about waist height” belongs inside the appositive because it tells you what kind of bench, so no punctuation may break it off.

whyWrong.A: With no comma at all, the appositive runs into the noun it renames and the sentence reads as though “banker a low bench” were one phrase.
whyWrong.C: Semicolons cannot introduce an appositive, and the second one cuts “set at about waist height” away from the bench it describes.
whyWrong.D: The extra comma after “timber” closes the appositive too early, stranding “set at about waist height” as a separate fragment.

tips: An appositive is punctuated as a unit: one mark in front, one at the end, nothing inside.

whyCorrect: “Because that mesh has no gaps of a fixed width and no grain to split along” is a subordinate clause, and “the first coat can be pressed into it…” is the main clause. When the subordinate clause comes first, a comma marks the boundary between them.

whyWrong.B: A semicolon joins two independent clauses; the “Because” clause is dependent and cannot stand on its own.
whyWrong.C: With no punctuation, “split along the first coat” reads as one phrase and the sentence loses its main clause.
whyWrong.D: A colon needs a complete sentence before it, and the “Because” clause is not one.

tips: Introductory dependent clause plus main clause equals comma — never a semicolon or colon.

whyCorrect: In a “there” construction the real subject follows the verb, and here it is “three foils and three cusps” — plural. The verb must therefore be plural. Tense is settled by the parallel clause after the semicolon, “in a quatrefoil there are four of each,” which is present, and by the fact that the text is describing what tracery always is.

whyWrong.B: “There is” is singular and cannot take a compound plural subject.
whyWrong.C: “There was” is both singular and past, clashing with the plural subject and with the present tense used throughout.
whyWrong.D: “There has been” is singular and present perfect, which treats a permanent definition as a completed development.

commonMistakes: Matching the verb to “there” instead of to the noun phrase that follows it.

whyCorrect: With “neither… nor,” the verb agrees with whichever subject is closer to it. The nearer subject here is “the head,” which is singular, so the verb is “plays.” The intervening phrase “carved on the outside” is a modifier and has no effect on agreement.

whyWrong.A: “Play” is plural. It would be right after “the wings” alone, but the proximity rule looks at “the head.”
whyWrong.C: “Have played” is plural and also shifts to the present perfect, which does not fit a general statement about how a gargoyle works.
whyWrong.D: “Are playing” is plural and puts a permanent fact into the progressive, as if it were happening only at the moment.

tips: For neither/nor and either/or, find the subject nearest the verb and match that one.

whyCorrect: The pronoun stands in for the sole board's job of spreading the weight resting on it, and its antecedent — “a timber sole board,” or the plate it carries — is singular. The possessive form of it is “its,” with no apostrophe.

whyWrong.B: “Their” is plural and has no plural antecedent; both “each plate” and “a timber sole board” are singular.
whyWrong.C: “It's” is the contraction of it is, which gives “spreads it is load.”
whyWrong.D: “Its'” is not a word in English in any position.

commonMistakes: Reaching for an apostrophe because the word is possessive; possessive pronouns never take one.

whyCorrect: The sentences before the blank list what torching did well: it kept driven snow out and stopped the tiles chattering in a gale. The sentence after it reports the opposite — the same mortar traps water against the battens and nails, and the timber beneath rots first. A benefit followed by the hidden cost of that same practice calls for a contrast transition.

whyWrong.A: “Therefore” claims the rot follows logically from the benefits, but rot is the drawback, not the consequence of keeping snow out.
whyWrong.C: “Likewise” signals another example of the same kind, and holding water against timber is not another benefit.
whyWrong.D: “In short” introduces a summary of what came before, but the new sentence adds information that cuts against it.

tips: When a sentence introduces a downside of what was just praised, the transition is contrastive.

whyCorrect: The sentence before the blank states a hazard: the shaft is open at every floor and anyone stepping in when the platform is elsewhere falls the full height. The sentence after describes the safeguard built to prevent exactly that — interlocked gates. Safeguard follows hazard as a consequence, so a result transition is what fits.

whyWrong.A: “Similarly” would make the gate a second instance of the danger rather than the response to it.
whyWrong.B: “Even so” is concessive, which would mean the gate exists despite the danger — the danger is the reason for it.
whyWrong.D: “For example” would make the gate an illustration of the hazard, but a gate is what stops the hazard.

tips: Hazard followed by precaution is a cause–effect pair, not a contrast.

whyCorrect: “Such a pattern carries nothing whatever” is the cause; the freedoms listed next — running straight across a beam, ignoring the shape of the room — are what a rib can do because it carries no load, which the sentence itself confirms with “as ribs bearing a load never could.” The blank therefore needs a consequence transition.

whyWrong.A: “In addition” treats the two sentences as separate points, hiding the fact that the second follows from the first.
whyWrong.B: “Nevertheless” sets up a contrast, but nothing in the second sentence works against carrying no load; it depends on it.
whyWrong.C: “For instance” would make crossing a beam an example of carrying nothing, whereas it is a result of carrying nothing.

tips: If you can insert “which is why” between the two sentences, the transition is a result word.

whyCorrect: The goal is to explain how the two tiles worked together, so the right choice has to describe both tiles and the relationship between them. Only this one does: the flanged tegulae laid side by side so their flanges met in pairs, and the half-round imbrex bedded over each pair to close the joint the flanges left. That is the interlock the question asks for.

whyWrong.A: It defines each tile separately but never says how they meet, so nothing is explained about how they worked together.
whyWrong.C: This is the most general note in the list and describes only the shapes, not the way one covers the other.
whyWrong.D: This explains why a flange keeps water out, which is a detail about one tile alone, not about the pair.

tips: Match the choice to the stated goal, not to whichever note is most interesting.

whyCorrect: The goal names the test: one tile, two purposes at once. This choice gives both — the hollow body carries the hot gas up inside the wall, and the comb-scored outer face keys the plaster — and joins them in a single sentence so the double duty is visible.

whyWrong.A: This describes only the heating function, so a reader learns one purpose, not two.
whyWrong.B: This reports the scoring but never says what the scoring achieves, so it names neither purpose completely.
whyWrong.D: This is a bare definition of the tile and mentions no purpose at all.

commonMistakes: Choosing a true note that covers half the goal; a “two purposes” prompt needs both stated in one sentence.

whyCorrect: The emphasis has to fall on what cleaning costs the surviving surface, which means linking two notes: the crust is formed out of the stone's own surface, so removing it removes original material, and the tooling marks lost with it cannot be replaced. This choice makes that chain explicit and ends on the irreversible loss.

whyWrong.A: It compares two cleaning methods but never says what is lost, so the cost to the surface goes unstated.
whyWrong.B: It explains how the crust forms in the air and says nothing about cleaning.
whyWrong.C: It identifies the crust as gypsum but stops short of the consequence — that taking it off takes the stone with it.

tips: When the goal is to emphasise a cost, pick the choice whose sentence actually ends on the loss.

whyCorrect: The blank has to name what the keyed plug of mortar does to the joint, and the sentence tells you which direction matters: “against movement along the bed.” Mortar pushed up into the frog sets into a block that a sliding force must break before the joint gives, so the joint resists being shifted sideways. That resistance to deformation is stiffness.

whyWrong.A: “Smoother” describes a surface, and a smoother joint would slide more easily, not less.
whyWrong.C: “Thinner” describes the amount of mortar; the frog adds mortar rather than reducing it, and thickness is not what resists sliding.
whyWrong.D: “Cheaper” is ruled out in the first sentence, which says the frog is not there to save clay.

tips: When a blank is followed by a prepositional phrase like “against movement,” the word must be one that phrase can attach to.

whyCorrect: The “not X but Y” frame means the blank must be the opposite of ornament, and the passage has already told you what the crossing bricks do: they reach from face to face and bind two half-walls into one member that will not split under load. A pattern that carries load is structure.

whyWrong.A: Repair implies fixing damage after the fact; the crossing bricks are laid as the wall is built.
whyWrong.B: Nothing in the text says the pattern is used to measure anything.
whyWrong.D: Decoration is a synonym for ornament, which the sentence explicitly rules out.

commonMistakes: Choosing the word that repeats the rejected half of “not… but…” instead of contrasting with it.

whyCorrect: In the ring kiln the chamber ahead of the fire is warmed by the gases drawn through it from the chamber that has just been burned. So the heat of a finished chamber is handed on to the next one instead of escaping as the kiln cools. “Inherited” captures that passing-on, and it is set against “not lost.”

whyWrong.B: “Discarded” is a synonym for lost, so it would contradict the “not lost but” contrast.
whyWrong.C: “Concealed” would mean the heat is hidden somewhere, but the text describes it doing useful work in the next chamber.
whyWrong.D: “Measured” describes recording a quantity, which no part of the passage mentions.

tips: After “not X but,” test each choice by asking whether it is genuinely the opposite of X.

whyCorrect: The whole passage is about a disguise: tiles cut and shadowed to pass for brick from the street. “Only at a corner, or where a tile has fallen” names the two places the disguise breaks down, so the blank must mean that the trick becomes visible. “Apparent” is that word.

whyWrong.A: “Profitable” concerns money, and cost is never raised in the text.
whyWrong.B: “Traditional” describes age or custom, not something a passer-by suddenly notices at a corner.
whyWrong.D: “Acceptable” concerns approval; the sentence is about whether the arrangement is detected.

tips: A blank introduced by “only where… does it become” almost always means “is noticed.”

whyCorrect: Follow the argument to its last sentence, which begins “in short” and states the point: the marks are the record a paymaster needed of who cut which stone. Everything before it clears the ground for that conclusion by ruling out decoration and citing accounts that name pieceworkers. The purpose is to explain what the marks were for.

whyWrong.A: The text denies the marks were decorative rather than arguing they were.
whyWrong.C: Accounts are mentioned once, as corroboration; no two cathedrals are compared.
whyWrong.D: The tools are never described — only that the figures are incised in a few strokes.

tips: When a text ends with “in short,” that sentence usually states the purpose outright.

whyCorrect: The underlined sentence states a fact about how the blocks were made: hollow, with thin webs across the void. The sentence after it does nothing but justify that choice — a solid block would dry slowly and crack in the fire, while a hollow one dries evenly, is light enough for one man, and can be filled with mortar afterwards. The underlined sentence introduces the feature those reasons explain.

whyWrong.B: Being hollow is presented as an advantage throughout; no defect is admitted and no remedy proposed.
whyWrong.C: The first sentence is about moulding, firing and ordering by the yard, and says nothing about hollowness.
whyWrong.D: No figure is given and no calculation follows.

tips: If the next sentence begins listing benefits or drawbacks, the underlined sentence is the thing being evaluated.

whyCorrect: Text 2 does not dispute that handmade tiles vary; it accepts the variation and then argues it “does work.” An uneven roof drains along many small channels and tolerates a rafter that has moved, while a machine tile laid on the same old timber has to be packed or the timber renewed. That is a functional defence, which is exactly the response to Text 1's charge that the variation is merely a failure to hold a size.

whyWrong.A: Text 2 opens by stating that handmade tiles vary by a few millimetres, so it cannot deny the variation.
whyWrong.B: Text 2 argues the variation is useful, not that it is a fault people have grown to like — and appearance is only its opening point.
whyWrong.D: Text 2 never discusses nib cracking; that detail belongs to Text 1's complaint about old roofs.

commonMistakes: Assuming the second author must reject the first author's facts. Here the facts are shared and only their significance is contested.

whyCorrect: The passage is a before-and-after built on one shift in thinking. Plate tracery cuts holes in a slab, and how big the holes can be is limited by how much solid panel can be removed before it fails. Bar tracery treats the window as a frame of separately cut, jointed bars, and the final sentence gives the payoff — the glass can grow until the whole bay between buttresses is window. The main idea has to include both the conceptual change and the size that follows from it.

whyWrong.A: Cost is never mentioned; the contrast is about what each method structurally permits.
whyWrong.B: The buttresses appear only as the limit of how wide the window can grow, not as something enlarged.
whyWrong.C: The text says the openings in a pierced slab stay small, not that such windows collapsed.

tips: A main-idea answer for a two-method passage should name the method and the consequence, not one alone.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences set up the whole point: the hair is not there to strengthen the hardened wall, and it does its work “in the hours before the coat has set at all.” The middle of the passage explains what that work is — wet stuff shrinks as water leaves, and fibre spreads that shrinkage instead of letting the coat tear open over every gap in the lath. So the idea is about controlling shrinkage before setting, not about final strength.

whyWrong.B: The text says a set coat carries its own weight perfectly well without hair, so setting does not depend on fibre.
whyWrong.C: Glass fibre is mentioned only as a modern material answering the same problem; nothing says it has displaced hair entirely.
whyWrong.D: No comparison of strength between coats appears anywhere in the passage.

commonMistakes: Assuming fibre in a material is always about strength; here the text explicitly rules that out in its second clause.

whyCorrect: Ferreira's claim has two parts: pantiles spread because they were lighter, and not because they were cheaper. Support therefore has to knock out the cost explanation and confirm the weight one. This finding does both — the accounts show the same cost per area, killing the cheapness account, while lighter rafters under pantiled roofs are the physical sign builders were exploiting reduced weight.

whyWrong.A: Colour range is an aesthetic difference and speaks to neither weight nor cost.
whyWrong.B: Later re-covering in slate says nothing about why pantiles were adopted in the seventeenth century.
whyWrong.C: Importation shows where the tiles came from, not why builders preferred them.

tips: When a claim says “because of X rather than Y,” the strongest support is evidence that rules Y out as well as evidence for X.

whyCorrect: Verner's claim is that a raking shore works or fails according to the level at which its head meets the wall, and not according to the size of the timber. This quotation says precisely that: bring the head to bear at a floor, where the joists can take the thrust, and a head landing between floors pushes on plaster and nothing else. It turns on height of bearing and never mentions timber size.

whyWrong.A: This is advice about how long a shore should be left standing, a different variable altogether.
whyWrong.C: This gives rules for the size of the timber — the very factor Verner says does not decide the matter, so it illustrates the opposite.
whyWrong.D: This concerns the ground under the foot of the shore, not the level at which its head meets the wall.

commonMistakes: Picking the quotation that mentions the same subject as the claim rather than the one that tests the claim's specific variable.

whyCorrect: Read the two data columns. Thickness runs 9 mm, 6 mm, 3 mm — each coat thinner than the last, matching the text's rule. The waiting times run 7 days then 10 days, so the longest wait is the one after the floating coat, which is the wait immediately before the 3 mm setting coat, the thinnest of the three. This choice states both facts accurately.

whyWrong.A: The last coat is 3 mm, the thinnest, not the thickest.
whyWrong.B: Both halves are reversed: the coats get thinner, and the wait lengthens from 7 days to 10.
whyWrong.D: The coats are 9, 6 and 3 mm, so they are not of equal thickness.

tips: On a two-column table, verify each half of the sentence separately before accepting a choice.

whyCorrect: Trace where the damage is generated. Water reaches the iron only where the lead run has been skimped, that is, in the cramp pockets. The rusting iron then expands to several times its original volume with nowhere to go except into the surrounding stone. Since the pressure originates in the pocket, the stone that splits first is the stone hemmed in around it, not the open face where no iron is buried.

whyWrong.A: Bed softness is never mentioned and would not explain damage concentrated at the joints.
whyWrong.B: Stone furthest from any joint is furthest from the expanding iron, so it is the least likely to go first.
whyWrong.C: The point of the passage is that expansion cracks the stone as the iron rusts; the crack does not wait until the metal is gone.

tips: For inference blanks, ask where the mechanism the passage describes actually applies force.

whyCorrect: The passage contrasts two states of the same frame. Open, it lets wind pass through and the ties hold little beyond the frame's own weight. Sheeted, it becomes a wall standing in the wind, so it collects wind pressure over its whole area. The ties were sized for the first condition, so sheeting an existing scaffold means the tie design has to be worked out again for the new load.

whyWrong.A: The load that matters is wind pressure on the new surface, not the weight of the sheeting itself — which is why its light weight is beside the point.
whyWrong.B: Removing ties would reduce restraint at the exact moment the frame gathers far more force.
whyWrong.D: A sheeted scaffold needs ties more than a bare one, not less.

commonMistakes: Judging the added load by the weight of the sheeting rather than by the wind area it creates.

whyCorrect: “A tingle” is a parenthetical appositive dropped into the middle of the sentence to name the tin plate. A non-essential element inside a sentence must be closed with the same kind of mark that opened it, so a dash in front requires a dash after.

whyWrong.B: Opening with a dash and closing with a comma mismatches the pair; the marks around an interrupter must match.
whyWrong.C: Same problem in the other order — a comma opens the insertion and a dash closes it.
whyWrong.D: With no closing mark at all, “a tingle is hooked over it” reads as the main clause and “a small tin plate” is left stranded.

tips: Cover the interrupter with your thumb: the sentence left behind must still read correctly, and the two marks you covered must match.

whyCorrect: Both halves here are complete sentences: “…the engineering bricks of south Staffordshire are blue” and “The colour is the whole record of how the fire was run.” Two independent clauses need a full stop, a semicolon, or a comma with a coordinating conjunction. Only the period is offered.

whyWrong.A: Running the clauses together with no punctuation produces a fused sentence.
whyWrong.B: “However” is a conjunctive adverb, not a coordinating conjunction, so a comma in front of it still leaves a splice — and the logic is continuation, not contrast.
whyWrong.D: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice.

commonMistakes: Treating “however” as if it worked like but. It cannot join two clauses with only a comma.

whyCorrect: “The shed cost the yard nothing to run” and “a week of still weather under it did more for a tile than any amount of care at the mould” are both independent clauses. Joining two of them takes a comma plus a coordinating conjunction, which is what “, and” supplies.

whyWrong.A: A comma with no conjunction between two independent clauses is a comma splice.
whyWrong.B: A semicolon already does the joining, so adding “and” after it doubles the connector.
whyWrong.D: Omitting the comma before “and” when it links two full clauses of this length runs them together.

tips: Check whether each side of the blank could stand alone as a sentence; if both can, you need one joining device, not none and not two.

whyCorrect: The rules belong to the masons of the lodge, more than one of them, so the noun is the plural “masons” and the possessive of a plural already ending in s is formed by adding an apostrophe alone: masons'. The context confirms the plural — the lodge is where the banker masons worked as a body.

whyWrong.A: “Masons's” is not a form English uses; a plural in s takes only the apostrophe.
whyWrong.B: “Mason's” is singular possessive, which would mean the rules of one individual mason rather than the trade's customs.
whyWrong.D: “Masons rules” drops the possessive marker altogether and leaves two nouns side by side.

tips: Decide the number of the owner first, then place the apostrophe: mason's for one, masons' for many.

whyCorrect: “Sliding the mould along the rule for the twentieth time” is a participial phrase, and the noun immediately after the comma has to be the one doing the sliding. A moulding cannot slide itself along a rule; the plasterer does. Putting “the plasterer” first fixes the modifier, and the rest of the clause reports what he found.

whyWrong.A: A profile does not slide the mould, so the modifier still dangles — and a profile is a shape, not a person.
whyWrong.C: This makes the moulding the slider, which reverses who is acting on what.
whyWrong.D: “It was the moulding that…” again attaches the sliding to the moulding rather than to a person.

commonMistakes: Choosing whichever option reads smoothly. With an opening participle, the only test is who or what performs that action.

whyCorrect: Find the head noun of the subject: “The rows of perforations pressed through the bed face of a modern brick.” The subject is “rows,” which is plural — “of perforations” is a prepositional phrase and cannot govern the verb. A plural subject takes “allow,” and the simple present matches the general statements around it.

whyWrong.A: “Has allowed” is singular and shifts to the present perfect, treating a permanent property as a past development.
whyWrong.B: “Is allowing” is singular and progressive, as if it were happening only right now.
whyWrong.D: “Allows” is singular; it agrees with “perforations” or “face” only if you mistake one of them for the subject.

tips: Cross out every prepositional phrase between the subject and the verb before checking agreement.

whyCorrect: The pronoun modifies “arrival” and refers back to “the keystone,” a singular thing, so it needs the singular possessive “its.” Possessive pronouns are written without an apostrophe.

whyWrong.A: “Their” is plural, but the keystone is one block — the text stresses that it is the single block placed last.
whyWrong.B: “Its'” is not a word in English.
whyWrong.C: “It's” means it is, giving “it is arrival is what allows,” which is not a sentence.

tips: Read the apostrophe version out in full as “it is”; if the sentence breaks, you need “its.”

whyCorrect: The sentence after the blank does not add new information. It restates the mechanics just described — thrust carried over the aisle to a free-standing pier and turned downward by a pinnacle — as a single compact formula: the buttress holds the vault in rather than the wall up. A restatement transition is what marks that move.

whyWrong.B: “For example” would require a specific instance, but the final sentence is more general than what precedes it, not less.
whyWrong.C: “Meanwhile” marks simultaneous events, and nothing here is happening at the same time as something else.
whyWrong.D: “Nevertheless” sets up a contrast, but the last sentence agrees with the paragraph and summarises it.

tips: If the final sentence could be introduced with “that is to say,” the answer is a restatement transition.

whyCorrect: The first half of the paragraph stresses separation: the gap keeps water from ever reaching the inner leaf. The sentence after the blank says that despite being kept apart in that way, the two leaves must behave as a single member against wind, so they are pinned together with ties. Separation set against required unity is a concession, so the transition has to be contrastive.

whyWrong.A: “For example” would make wall ties an instance of rain drainage, which they are not.
whyWrong.B: “As a result” claims the ties follow from the drainage, but the ties exist in spite of the gap, not because of it.
whyWrong.C: “Likewise” signals a parallel point, and structural behaviour under wind is a different matter from water exclusion.

commonMistakes: Reading any two facts about one object as if the second must follow from the first.

whyCorrect: The sentence before the blank establishes that ashlar takes hours of bench work rubble never gets and that the wall costs accordingly. The sentence after reports builders using ashlar only on the visible faces and rubble behind. That is exactly what you would predict from the cost difference, so the transition should mark the sentence as the expected consequence.

whyWrong.A: “Even so” would signal that the practice runs against the cost pressure, when it follows straight from it.
whyWrong.B: “For example” would make this an instance of high cost, but it is a response to high cost.
whyWrong.D: “Instead” announces a replacement for something just rejected, and nothing has been rejected.

tips: Ask whether the next sentence is what you would have guessed. If yes, the transition confirms rather than contrasts.

whyCorrect: The goal is to say why a toe board is needed in addition to a guard rail, which means naming the different hazard each one answers. Only this choice does: the rail catches the worker who overbalances, and the low board along the edge stops material being kicked off onto people below. Two hazards, two devices.

whyWrong.B: This gives the heights of both but never says what either prevents, so it does not explain why both are needed.
whyWrong.C: It names the two hazards without connecting either to the rail or to the board.
whyWrong.D: It states when guarding is required at all, which says nothing about the division of work between the two devices.

tips: When the goal contains “as well as,” the answer must give a distinct job for each item.

whyCorrect: The goal is the practical advantage, so the answer has to name a benefit and support it with the contrast in the notes. This choice does: because the ribs are built first and then carry the webs, the centring need only hold up the arches, whereas a groin vault's centring must hold the whole bay at once. That is a real saving in timber and labour, and it is stated so a newcomer can follow it.

whyWrong.A: Defining the webs is background; no advantage is claimed.
whyWrong.C: This describes the groin vault alone and states no benefit of the rib vault.
whyWrong.D: This defines the rib vault accurately but stops before saying what is gained by building it that way.

commonMistakes: Selecting a correct definition instead of the choice that answers the goal's word “advantage.”

whyCorrect: To emphasise scale you need the two numbers set against each other: a gang of only four or five men against an output of four to five thousand bricks in a single working day. This is the only choice that carries the output figure at all, and it places it next to the size of the team so the reader feels the ratio.

whyWrong.B: This describes one man's task and mentions no quantity of bricks.
whyWrong.C: This lists the roles in the gang but leaves out the daily output entirely.
whyWrong.D: This describes the moulding and carrying operation without any figure for how much was produced.

tips: If the goal is to emphasise scale, the answer almost always has to include the number.

whyCorrect: The sentence ends “rather than the exception,” so the blank needs the word that stands opposite an exception — the normal case. That matches the change described: before Ward's case almost every consignment died, and after it a sealed box needed no attention for months, so plants surviving became the ordinary outcome.

whyWrong.A: An argument is a claim someone makes; survival is an outcome, not a position taken.
whyWrong.C: A hazard is a danger, which describes the old conditions rather than the new reliability.
whyWrong.D: Expense concerns cost, and the passage credits the case with reducing attention, not with money.

tips: “Rather than the exception” is a fixed frame; the blank is always a word meaning “the usual case.”

whyCorrect: The sentence sets up a contrast: pressure alone gives a flat brown specimen, but steady removal of water leaves the colour something better. So the blank must name the good outcome — the colour preserved rather than turned brown. “Intact” is that word.

whyWrong.A: “Uniform” means evenly the same throughout, which a brown specimen also is; it does not signal preservation.
whyWrong.B: “Faded” describes colour lost, the failure the technique avoids.
whyWrong.D: “Muted” also means dulled, so it sits on the wrong side of the contrast.

commonMistakes: Missing that the semicolon divides a bad result from a good one, and choosing a second word for the bad result.

whyCorrect: The blank is judged from the collector's position: he is working far from a laboratory. The passage contrasts the tin with refrigerated machinery that is expensive and “stops when the current does,” while the gel dries the air and signals its own exhaustion by changing colour, needing neither power nor an instrument. Its merit for that user is that it depends on nothing else.

whyWrong.A: Durability would be about how long the tin lasts physically, which the text never raises.
whyWrong.C: Capacity is how much water the gel can hold, and the text mentions capacity only as a limit that the colour change announces.
whyWrong.D: Precision would mean an accurate measurement, but the colour change is a rough signal, not a reading.

tips: When a blank names a “chief merit,” check which quality the passage contrasts with a stated alternative.

whyCorrect: Passing steam through a loosely packed charge keeps the plant material off the hot metal, so the scorching never happens in the first place. The blank must therefore mean prevented in advance, and the closing clause — a fault no later rectification could remove — is the reason it has to be headed off rather than repaired afterwards. “Forestall” means exactly that.

whyWrong.A: “Tolerate” means to put up with the fault, the opposite of redesigning the process to avoid it.
whyWrong.B: “Disguise” would mean hiding the burnt note, but the change removes the cause of it.
whyWrong.D: “Diagnose” means to identify a problem, and the problem was already known.

tips: A clause saying a fault cannot be fixed later points the blank toward prevention.

whyCorrect: The passage keeps inverting the expected hierarchy: the label is what makes the plant evidence, and every later use of the sheet — mapping, dating, naming — draws on the slip rather than on the plant. So the closing sentence makes the plant the secondary thing attached to the label. “Appendage” names something attached and subordinate, which is the joke the sentence is making.

whyWrong.A: An objection would mean the plant argues against its label, and nothing suggests conflict between them.
whyWrong.B: An improvement would make the plant the better of the two, reversing the passage's point.
whyWrong.C: An alternative would mean the plant could be used instead of the label, but the text says the uses depend on the label.

tips: When a passage repeatedly says B does the work and A does not, the closing metaphor makes A subordinate to B.

whyCorrect: The underlined sentence begins “The arrangement survives because…,” which is an explicit answer to why the seed exchange has lasted two centuries: neither the surplus given nor the wants requested costs a garden anything. The sentence after it illustrates that with a curator sending away ninety spare seeds and losing no advantage. So its job is to name the feature that explains the practice's persistence.

whyWrong.A: No weakness is conceded; the sentence names a strength, and nothing is said about later correction.
whyWrong.B: The commercial trade is never mentioned; the text notes only that no money passes.
whyWrong.C: The accuracy of the catalogues is not questioned anywhere.

tips: A sentence beginning “X survives because” is stating a cause, so look for the choice with a causal verb.

whyCorrect: The underlined sentence states the general principle — the seed responds to change, not to warmth itself. The sentence before it is a concrete case of that principle (cabinets run on a sixteen-hour and eight-hour cycle because species answer the day–night swing), and the sentence after is another (a constant twenty degrees carries no information, a daily swing does). Illustration, principle, illustration.

whyWrong.B: Cabinets are not being criticised; the text explains how they are run so that they work.
whyWrong.C: It agrees with the first sentence, which reports that steady-temperature cabinets fail to sprout seed.
whyWrong.D: No term is defined; “measuring” is used figuratively rather than given a specialised sense.

tips: If the sentences on both sides are specific and the underlined one is general, it is the principle they illustrate.

whyCorrect: The question asks why the confusion was particularly serious in dispensing, and the last clause answers it directly: the error was one “no arithmetic later in the prescription would reveal.” An ordinary mistake shows up when the figures are checked; this one passes every check, which is what makes it dangerous.

whyWrong.A: Nothing says troy was being withdrawn; both systems are described as in daily use.
whyWrong.B: Drugs and goods being sold in one shop explains how the mix-up could happen, not why its consequences were severe.
whyWrong.C: The text says the troy ounce is the heavier of the two — the weights differ, and the problem is detection, not the balance.

commonMistakes: Answering “how did the error occur” when the question asks “why was it serious.”

whyCorrect: The passage describes a practice with a motive of its own — posting identical numbered sets across Europe — and then names a consequence nobody planned. The final sentence calls it “an unintended value”: when a herbarium burned, its sheets were seldom unique. The main idea must include both the practice and the incidental protection it produced.

whyWrong.B: This reverses the causation. The text calls the protection unintended, so it cannot have been the chief purpose.
whyWrong.C: The text says several herbaria burned, not that most nineteenth-century material was destroyed — the point is the opposite.
whyWrong.D: No claim is made that uniqueness confers value; the passage treats duplication as an advantage.

tips: The word “unintended” is a warning against any choice that turns the effect into the motive.

whyCorrect: The claim is about one stage in particular: winnowing took out material that screening had missed. Only the pair of readings that brackets the winnowing step tests it — 31.9 grams after screening and 35.6 grams after winnowing. That rise of 3.7 grams per thousand seeds happened after screening was finished, so it is light rubbish screening left behind.

whyWrong.A: A rise at every stage is true but does not isolate winnowing; it would equally support a claim about any other stage.
whyWrong.C: The starting weight of the uncleaned lot says nothing about which stage removed what.
whyWrong.D: The gravity table figure concerns a later stage and, if anything, describes how little that stage added.

tips: To support a claim about one step, quote the values immediately before and immediately after that step.

whyCorrect: The claim is about the bulk of the oil coming over early, so it needs the first hour weighed against the rest of the run. The first hour gave 310 millilitres; the remaining three gave 96 + 24 + 9 = 129 millilitres. 310 is more than twice 129, so the opening hour alone outweighs the rest of the run put together — exactly the comparison the claim requires.

whyWrong.A: That the last hour is smallest tells you the yield tails off but not that most of the oil came early.
whyWrong.B: A falling trend shows decline without showing what share the first hour holds.
whyWrong.C: 96 does exceed 24 + 9, but this compares the middle of the run with its end and never mentions the first hour.

commonMistakes: Settling for a choice that shows a decreasing trend when the claim is about proportion and needs an actual comparison of totals.

whyCorrect: The chemist's proposal is that a normal reading cannot by itself prove purity. What breaks the test is a case where an adulterated sample gives the pure oil's own reading. Two diluents that cancel each other's effect do precisely that: the sample is impure yet the polarimeter shows the characteristic angle, so a good reading no longer rules adulteration out.

whyWrong.A: Readings far outside the pure range are cases where the polarimeter succeeds in catching adulteration, which supports the test rather than limiting it.
whyWrong.C: Slight temperature sensitivity affects precision and can be corrected for; it does not let an adulterated sample imitate a pure one.
whyWrong.D: Old instruments being less precise is a fact about hardware, not about what the measurement can establish in principle.

tips: To undermine a test, look for the false negative — the impure sample that passes.

whyCorrect: The sentence explains why the old dates are trustworthy: the collectors “were not thinking about the question at all.” The question in view throughout the passage is whether flowering has shifted. So the contrast is between a date written merely to identify a specimen and a date written to prove a shift, which would carry the writer's expectations with it.

whyWrong.B: A date is not used to tell species apart, and separating species is not the question the researchers are asking.
whyWrong.C: Locality is a separate field on the label, and recording it would not bias a date.
whyWrong.D: The collector's name is also a separate item, and no expectation about flowering attaches to it.

tips: When a passage praises evidence for being disinterested, the blank names the purpose that would have made it interested.

whyCorrect: Weigh what the instrument can and cannot do. It is fast — one drop, a reading in seconds — but it will not name the adulterant, and two adulterants can move the reading in opposite directions, so a normal figure does not clear a sample. A fast test that cannot convict or acquit on its own is a screen: it tells you which samples to examine properly.

whyWrong.A: The text says outright that the figure will not name what has been added.
whyWrong.B: Proportion cannot be inferred when different adulterants shift the reading in opposite directions.
whyWrong.C: That is the false negative the passage warns about — opposing shifts can cancel, so a normal reading proves nothing.

commonMistakes: Treating a quick instrument as a verdict. Speed makes it a first filter, not a proof.

whyCorrect: Everything before the blank is already a complete compound sentence — two clauses about early cutting and late cutting joined by “and.” “Growers watch the field daily through the fortnight in between” is a third independent clause. Two independent clauses need a semicolon or a period, and only the semicolon is offered.

whyWrong.A: A comma alone between independent clauses is a comma splice, and the sentence already uses a comma for its first join.
whyWrong.B: With no punctuation the two clauses fuse into a run-on.
whyWrong.C: “And which” turns the second half into a relative clause with nothing to attach to, since “growers watch” already has its own subject and verb.

tips: Count the subject–verb pairs. Three independent clauses need two joining devices, and “and” only covers one of them.

whyCorrect: “The shoot that will bear the fruit is called the scion” and “the root it is joined to is called the stock” are both complete clauses, and the sentence goes on to add a third with “, and the two may come…” A semicolon is the mark that separates the first two while keeping the parallel definitions in one sentence.

whyWrong.A: Joining two independent clauses with a bare “and” and no comma runs them together, and the sentence then has two coordinating “and”s doing different jobs.
whyWrong.C: A comma with no conjunction is a splice.
whyWrong.D: No punctuation at all produces a fused sentence — “the scion the root” reads as a single noun phrase.

tips: When two clauses define paired terms, a semicolon keeps the parallel visible.

whyCorrect: The sentence is a series of three independent clauses describing successive steps: sheets are gathered into a folder, the folders are stacked in fascicles, and the fascicles are shelved. Items in a series are separated by commas, with the conjunction before the last one, so the blank needs a comma to match the comma already placed after “folder.”

whyWrong.B: A semicolon in the third position breaks the parallel punctuation of the series, since the first join is a comma.
whyWrong.C: A period would leave the earlier comma joining two independent clauses on its own, producing a splice.
whyWrong.D: With no punctuation, “stacked in fascicles and the fascicles are shelved” runs the second and third steps together.

tips: When three or more clauses list steps in order, punctuate them like any other series.

whyCorrect: “Held at twenty degrees below freezing for four days” is a single uninterrupted phrase: “for four days” tells you how long the sheet is held, so it belongs with the verb and nothing may be inserted before it. The blank takes no punctuation.

whyWrong.A: A colon must follow a complete clause and introduce something; here it would cut the temperature off from the duration.
whyWrong.C: A comma separates the verb phrase from the time phrase that completes it, with no reason for the pause.
whyWrong.D: A semicolon requires an independent clause on each side, and “for four days before it goes to the shelf” is not one.

commonMistakes: Adding punctuation because the sentence is long. Punctuation marks structure, not breathing.

whyCorrect: The clause introduced by “while” needs its own finite verb: the subject is “one” (a label struck into lead or zinc), so the verb must be a conjugated form. “Outlasts” is singular to match “one” and present tense to match “lasts” in the first half of the comparison.

whyWrong.A: “Outlasting” is a participle, not a finite verb, so the “while” clause is left without a predicate.
whyWrong.B: “To outlast” is an infinitive and likewise cannot serve as the clause's verb.
whyWrong.C: “Having outlasted” is another participle form and also shifts the time frame of a general statement.

tips: If a subordinate clause has a subject but no conjugated verb, the blank must supply one.

whyCorrect: The subject is the noun clause “what it does,” which is singular, so the linking verb is “is.” The construction “what it does is slow the loss of water” is a standard cleft, and the bare infinitive after it is correct because the clause already contains the verb do.

whyWrong.B: “Are” is plural; a “what” clause of this kind takes a singular verb.
whyWrong.C: “Being” is a participle and leaves the sentence with no main verb after the semicolon.
whyWrong.D: “To be” is an infinitive and cannot serve as the main verb of the clause.

tips: A sentence starting “What it does” is a cleft; the verb that follows is always singular is.

whyCorrect: The subject is “the two products” — the volatile oil and the rosin — which is plural, so the verb must be plural. The present tense also matches the general statements running through the rest of the sentence.

whyWrong.B: “Is” is singular and cannot take a plural subject.
whyWrong.C: “Was being” is singular and past progressive, turning a permanent fact about the trade into something that happened for a while.
whyWrong.D: “Being” is a participle, so the clause after “and” would have no finite verb at all.

tips: “The two” is always plural, however singular the following noun looks.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences establish that citrus oil is never steamed but pressed out cold. The sentence after the blank reports what follows from that: waxes and pigments stay in the oil, because nothing has distilled them away. Cause then effect, so the transition marks a consequence.

whyWrong.A: “In other words” would make the last sentence a restatement, but it introduces new content about waxes and pigments.
whyWrong.C: “In spite of this” sets up a contrast; the waxes are present precisely because of cold pressing, not despite it.
whyWrong.D: “Meanwhile” marks something happening at the same time elsewhere, which does not describe this relationship.

tips: If the last sentence names a property produced by the method just described, the transition is causal.

whyCorrect: The first sentence says a child-resistant closure has to demand two simultaneous motions; the second says those same motions defeat many arthritic adults. The sentence after the blank draws the conclusion that follows from putting the two together: the most protective design is one some households cannot open. That is a deduction, so a result transition is needed.

whyWrong.A: “Instead” introduces a substitute for something rejected, and nothing has been rejected.
whyWrong.B: “Previously” marks time order, but the last sentence is a conclusion, not an earlier event.
whyWrong.D: “Otherwise” means “if that were not so,” which reverses the logic — the conclusion holds because the two facts are so.

tips: When the final sentence combines two earlier facts into one consequence, use a result word.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences give the nose's strength and then its limit: it cannot say what the adulterant is or how much is present. The sentence after the blank describes an instrument that does exactly those two things — separates the components and reports the size of each. The blank marks the switch from a method that lacks a capability to one that has it.

whyWrong.A: “Likewise” claims similarity, but the chromatograph is introduced for what it does differently.
whyWrong.B: “For instance” would make the chromatograph an example of a trained nose, which it is not.
whyWrong.C: “In short” introduces a summary, and the last sentence adds a new method rather than condensing what came before.

tips: A stated limitation followed by something that lacks that limitation is a contrast.

whyCorrect: The goal is what the garden added to the books, so the answer has to name the books' shortcoming and the garden's remedy in one movement. This choice does both: a written description could fit more than one plant in the field, and the labelled beds with a demonstrator naming each plant gave a direct acquaintance students carried into practice. That is the gap and the thing that filled it.

whyWrong.A: It describes the garden fully but never mentions the textbooks, so nothing is shown to have been added.
whyWrong.B: It sets a fact about textbooks next to a fact about the beds without connecting them, leaving the reader to supply the point.
whyWrong.C: Both halves are about the weakness of descriptions; the garden never appears.

tips: When the goal says “what X added to Y,” the answer must contain both X and Y and the relation between them.

whyCorrect: The goal is a benefit to the lending herbarium, so the answer must end with something the lender gains. Only this choice does: sheets go out to a specialist revising the group and come back carrying a new determination slip, so the collection has its material identified by an expert it does not pay. That is the return on the loan.

whyWrong.B: This explains the administrative rules of lending and names no gain to the lender.
whyWrong.C: This describes the scale of a loan but stops before saying what comes back.
whyWrong.D: It mentions the determination slip but pairs it with a procedural note instead of stating the benefit, so the point is left unmade.

commonMistakes: Choosing a choice that contains the right detail without drawing the conclusion the goal asks for.

whyCorrect: The goal is why the envelope is worth attaching, so the answer needs a payoff. This choice gives the immediate purpose — loose seeds and fragments stay with the specimen that produced them — and then the strongest evidence of value in the notes: material can be removed, examined and replaced, and seeds have germinated a century after collection.

whyWrong.A: It reports two procedural facts and never says what is gained by them.
whyWrong.C: This describes the envelope and its numbering, which is how it works rather than why it is worth the trouble.
whyWrong.D: It explains why glue will not serve, which is a reason the envelope is used, not a statement of its value.

tips: For a “why is it worth it” goal, prefer the choice that ends on the outcome, not on the procedure.

whyCorrect: The sentence before the blank supplies the reason: any failure could be blamed on the preparation or the practitioner, so no result ever counted against the doctrine. A rule that no observation can contradict cannot be checked, and the passage has already said it “offered no way of finding out that it was wrong.” The blank must therefore mean unable to be put to a test.

whyWrong.A: The text says the opposite — the rule's memorability was “a great deal of its attraction.”
whyWrong.B: It appeared in written herbals, and whether it was written down is not what the reason clause is about.
whyWrong.C: “Unremarkable” describes how interesting the doctrine is, not whether evidence could bear on it.

tips: When a passage says every failure can be explained away, the blank is about testability.

whyCorrect: The vessel takes a mixture of oil floating on water and has two outlets, one at the neck for the lighter layer and one at the foot for the heavier. Nothing is changed chemically; the two liquids are simply drawn off from different places. That is separation.

whyWrong.A: Purification suggests improving the oil itself, but the sentence explicitly rules out any chemistry.
whyWrong.B: Nothing is measured; the outlets divide the layers, they do not gauge them.
whyWrong.C: Storage would mean holding the mixture, whereas the outlets exist to get the two components out.

tips: When a device has two outlets at different heights and a mixture of two densities, its job is to divide them.

whyCorrect: The passage denies any ornamental intention and describes beds arranged so that a student walking the paths meets the plants in the order the lecturer treats them. The closing clause — built so that the ground itself would hold the lesson together — makes the garden a device for instruction, so the blank names a piece of teaching equipment.

whyWrong.B: Civic display is about impressing the public, which the sentence rules out by denying ornament.
whyWrong.C: Private recreation contradicts a layout organised around a lecture course for students.
whyWrong.D: A commercial nursery grows plants to sell, and nothing in the text concerns trade.

tips: A sentence that denies decoration is setting up a functional word in the blank; find the function the passage describes.

whyCorrect: The sentence names a specific situation: a hand reaching along a dark shelf at night meets the ridges before it lifts the bottle. In the dark, the colour is useless and the label unreadable, so what identifies the bottle is the feel of the ribbing under the fingers.

whyWrong.A: Smell would require opening the bottle, and the ribbing has nothing to do with odour.
whyWrong.C: The dark blue is mentioned, but the sentence explains the ribbing, and colour cannot be seen on a dark shelf at night.
whyWrong.D: Weight is never mentioned and the hand meets the ridges before it even lifts the bottle.

commonMistakes: Picking colour because the passage mentions blue glass. Read which feature the sentence with the blank is explaining.

whyCorrect: The fixed fact is the ratio: about three tonnes of petals per kilogram of oil, and no skill at the still changes it. Those petals have to be picked by hand before the sun is high and processed the same day, so the cost that dominates is the enormous amount of hand-picking behind every kilogram. That is what the blank must name.

whyWrong.A: Fuel is never mentioned, and the passage attributes the cost to the quantity of flowers rather than to running the still.
whyWrong.C: The still's design belongs to the distiller's art, which the sentence explicitly sets aside.
whyWrong.D: Season length is not discussed; the constraint stated is picking early in the day and distilling the same day.

tips: “Less by X than by” means the blank must be something other than X — here, other than the distiller's skill.

whyCorrect: The last sentence sets the boundary explicitly: the designated specimen settles nothing about how wide the species should be drawn, only which plant the name is anchored to. The passage exists to draw that line — what the type sheet decides and what it leaves open.

whyWrong.A: No pressing, mounting or storage procedure is described anywhere.
whyWrong.B: Nothing is recommended; the text describes existing practice with a single designated sheet.
whyWrong.D: Descriptions are called incomplete as a matter of fact, which is the reason for using a specimen, not a complaint about botanists.

tips: When a text ends with “it settles only…,” its purpose is usually to mark the limits of something.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences set one material against another: paper passes water vapour without limit, so seed drifts to room humidity, while a foil laminate with a heat-sealed seam does not. The last two sentences then say exactly what the better packet achieves — not drying the seed, but fixing the dryness it had when sealed. Contrast, then a precise statement of the benefit.

whyWrong.A: No sequence of operations is given; two materials are compared.
whyWrong.B: No data appear at all, and the closing sentences sharpen the claim rather than qualify it with figures.
whyWrong.C: No term is defined and no change of meaning over time is traced.

tips: A closing sentence beginning “It does not X. It does Y” is a precision move, not a qualification.

whyCorrect: The passage says the wall takes in heat all day and releases it at night, so the air beside it never drops as far as the air in the open. The last clause is the key: the plants “were not hardier there; the frost simply reached them later and left them sooner.” The wall changes the plants' surroundings, not the plants, and that is the main idea.

whyWrong.A: No abandonment of tender fruit is mentioned; the text describes gardeners succeeding with it.
whyWrong.C: The text denies this outright — the plants were not hardier.
whyWrong.D: Wind shelter is named in the first sentence only to be set aside as less than what the wall really does.

commonMistakes: Choosing the wind-shelter option because it is the familiar reason for a garden wall; the passage opens by moving past it.

whyCorrect: The question asks for the drawback of spirit, and the last sentence gives it directly: the jars take a hundred times the shelf space of a sheet and cannot be posted. That is why nothing goes into spirit unless the press would ruin it.

whyWrong.A: Cost is never mentioned in the passage.
whyWrong.B: Both kinds of preservation carry data in the text's account; the limitation stated is space and posting, not labelling.
whyWrong.D: The text says the opposite — material in spirit holds its shape and something of its colour indefinitely.

tips: When a question asks why something is not used for everything, look for the sentence listing its costs.

whyCorrect: The proposal is that sheets record the air of the district where the plant grew. Support has to show a sheet's chemistry tracking a known difference in air. This finding does: same species, same year, different places, and sulphur markedly higher in the sheets from downwind of coal-burning towns. Holding species and year constant is what makes the place the only variable left.

whyWrong.B: Better locality labelling makes the archive easier to use but shows nothing about whether the leaves record the air.
whyWrong.C: A bias in which species were collected is a limitation of the archive, not evidence that it records air quality.
whyWrong.D: A fall in atmospheric sulphur is a fact about the air itself, measured independently; it says nothing about what the sheets carry.

tips: The strongest support holds every variable fixed except the one the claim depends on.

whyCorrect: The claim is about diminishing returns at the dry end, so it needs two step sizes compared. Going from 9 to 7 per cent moisture lifts germination from 54 to 88, a gain of 34 points; going from 7 to 5 per cent lifts it only from 88 to 91, a gain of 3 points. The same two-point reduction in moisture buys far less once the seed is already dry, which is exactly the claim.

whyWrong.A: The worst result at the wet end shows drying helps, not that its benefit tails off.
whyWrong.B: A rise at every step establishes the direction of the effect but not that the size of the effect shrinks.
whyWrong.D: The highest figure alone gives no comparison, so no diminishing return can be read from it.

commonMistakes: Supporting “the benefit falls away” with a choice about the overall trend. The claim is about the size of each step, so two steps must be compared.

whyCorrect: The historian says the register was a defence against later dispute rather than a stock record. This entry is written like evidence for a future challenge: it names the recipient, cites the prescriber's order by date, notes that the order itself is pinned into the book, and records a witness. None of that helps with stock; all of it helps if the transaction is later questioned.

whyWrong.A: Recording a quantity made up and where it was placed is stock-keeping, which is the account the historian rejects.
whyWrong.B: Goods received from a wholesaler is a purchase record, again stock rather than defence.
whyWrong.C: A note about a cracked mortar concerns equipment and bears on neither purpose.

tips: For a “kept as a defence” claim, look for corroboration — a witness, a retained document, an authority cited.

whyCorrect: Before assaying, a dose written by weight of leaf was really a dose of an unknown amount of active substance, since leaves from two hillsides could differ several-fold. An assay measures the strength of the material, so the physician can now specify how much drug the patient receives rather than how much plant matter. That is the change in what a prescription means.

whyWrong.A: Ease of writing is not what changed; the difficulty was that the written figure did not correspond to a known quantity.
whyWrong.B: Season is never mentioned; the variation described is between places, and the assay handles variation from any source.
whyWrong.D: Cost is not discussed anywhere in the passage.

tips: When a text contrasts an unknown quantity with a measured one, the inference is about what the number now refers to.

whyCorrect: Two facts combine. Cold stops the beetles long before it harms the seed, and a long-term store is already held at a temperature at which the beetles do not breed. So the store needs no separate insect programme — the conditions it keeps for the seed's sake happen to stop the weevils as well.

whyWrong.A: Nothing limits the effect to one season; the cold is maintained for as long as the seed is held.
whyWrong.C: Fumigation is never mentioned, and the passage's point is that the temperature already does the work.
whyWrong.D: The temperature is the very condition that keeps the seed alive for decades, so it costs the seed nothing.

tips: When one condition serves two purposes, the inference is usually that the second comes free.

whyCorrect: “The Society of Apothecaries leased four acres… and planted them for the instruction of its apprentices” is one complete clause, and “the ground is still a garden today” is another. Two independent clauses cannot sit together without a joining device; the semicolon supplies it and keeps the two closely related facts in one sentence.

whyWrong.A: With nothing between them the clauses fuse into a run-on.
whyWrong.B: “And” with no comma before it runs two full clauses together; a coordinating conjunction joining independent clauses needs the comma.
whyWrong.D: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a splice.

tips: Read from the blank to the end. If what follows has its own subject and verb, a comma will not do.

whyCorrect: Both halves stand alone: “Vapour leaving the still head passes into a copper pipe coiled inside a tub of running water” and “by the time it reaches the foot of the coil it has condensed to a liquid.” A semicolon is the only offered mark that can join two independent clauses.

whyWrong.A: No punctuation at all leaves a fused sentence, and “running water by the time” reads as a single phrase.
whyWrong.B: “But” needs a comma before it, and the relationship is sequential rather than contrastive — condensation is what the cold water is for.
whyWrong.D: A comma without a conjunction is a comma splice.

commonMistakes: Assuming a long introductory phrase in the second clause (“by the time…”) makes it dependent. It still contains a subject and a verb of its own.

whyCorrect: “Heat from a brick flue… kept the tubs of citrus above freezing through the winter” and “the smoke was carried out through the far wall” are both independent clauses. The standard way to join them is a comma followed by a coordinating conjunction, which is what “, and” gives.

whyWrong.A: With no punctuation the two clauses run together.
whyWrong.C: “And” without the comma is not enough to join two full clauses of this length.
whyWrong.D: A comma with no conjunction is a splice.

tips: Comma plus conjunction is one device. Using only one half of it leaves the join incomplete.

whyCorrect: The first sentence is already a three-part series ending with the porcelain clause, and “Iron tainted acid preparations and fell out of use” is a separate independent clause with its own subject. A period closes the series cleanly and starts the new statement about iron.

whyWrong.B: A comma here creates a splice, and it also reads as though iron were a fourth item in the series rather than a new clause.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon followed by “and” doubles the connector, and it hangs a new clause off a sentence that has already closed its series.
whyWrong.D: “Mortar and iron tainted acid preparations” makes mortar and iron a compound subject, which reverses the meaning — porcelain is the material that worked.

tips: When the new clause introduces a different subject and a different verdict, start a new sentence.

whyCorrect: The clause after “and” needs a finite verb, and its subject is the gerund phrase “bottling it,” which is singular. “Makes” is the singular present form and matches “holds” in the parallel clause before it.

whyWrong.A: “To make” is an infinitive and leaves the clause without a predicate.
whyWrong.C: “Make” is plural; a gerund subject takes a singular verb.
whyWrong.D: “Making” is a participle, so the clause would have two -ing forms and no working verb.

tips: A gerund phrase used as a subject is always singular, however many nouns it contains.

whyCorrect: The word is the plain plural subject of “are checked,” and it owns nothing, so no apostrophe belongs on it. The plural verb “are” confirms the subject must be plural: the jars nearest the door are checked first.

whyWrong.A: “Jars'” is a plural possessive, but nothing after it is being possessed.
whyWrong.B: “Jar” is singular and clashes with the plural verb “are checked.”
whyWrong.D: “Jar's” is both singular and possessive, wrong on both counts.
