tips: An apostrophe marks ownership, not plurality. If no following noun is owned, drop it.

whyCorrect: Strip the prepositional phrase: the subject is “the small weights,” not “set.” A plural subject takes “are,” and the present tense matches “are lifted” in the second half of the sentence.

whyWrong.A: “Was” is singular and past, clashing with both the plural subject and the present tense used after the comma.
whyWrong.B: “Has been” is singular and shifts to the present perfect for what is a standing practice.
whyWrong.D: “Is” agrees with “set,” which is inside a prepositional phrase and cannot be the subject.

commonMistakes: Letting the noun closest to the verb decide agreement. Cross out “of an apothecary's set” and the plural subject is obvious.

whyCorrect: The sentence before the blank describes the method — standing the pots out for a few hours a day over a fortnight — and the sentence after states what the method accomplishes: the tissues harden while the plant can still be rescued indoors. A transition marking manner or means is what links a procedure to its effect.

whyWrong.A: “Even so” is concessive, but the hardening is the intended result of the practice, not something happening despite it.
whyWrong.B: “By contrast” needs two opposed things, and the last sentence agrees with the one before it.
whyWrong.C: “Beforehand” would place the hardening earlier in time, whereas it happens during the fortnight described.

tips: When the last sentence explains what the described procedure achieves, look for a means transition such as “in this way.”

whyCorrect: The second sentence grants that cold dry storage slows the staling of oily seed. The sentence after the blank says that even under identical conditions the oily seed still fails before the starchy one, which cuts against any impression that good storage evens the two out. A concession followed by a persisting difference calls for a contrast transition.

whyWrong.A: “For example” would make the failure an instance of storage slowing decay, but it is a limit on that effect.
whyWrong.B: “In addition” treats it as another supporting point when it works against the preceding sentence.
whyWrong.D: “Therefore” claims the earlier failure follows from good storage, which reverses the relationship.

tips: If the new sentence contains “still” or “anyway,” a contrast transition is usually what precedes it.

whyCorrect: The passage says the run is split into three portions and treated differently: the first and last are set aside or redistilled, and only the middle is bottled as it stands. Portions of unequal quality command unequal prices, so the last sentence states the consequence of that sorting. The transition must mark a result.

whyWrong.B: “Even so” would mean the different prices happen despite the sorting, when they follow from it.
whyWrong.C: “In contrast” needs opposition, and the last sentence agrees with what precedes it.
whyWrong.D: “Similarly” claims a parallel between two separate cases, but only one practice is under discussion.

tips: Sorting a product into grades leads directly to differing prices — that is a cause–effect link, not a contrast.

whyCorrect: The goal is to explain why clary sage became a field crop for a reader who knows no perfumery, so the answer needs the whole chain. This choice supplies it: the oil contains sclareol, sclareol converts to a substitute for ambergris, ambergris was scarce and costly, and a fixative slows the evaporation of a perfume's lighter parts. Every link a newcomer needs is present and in order.

whyWrong.A: It pairs the crop with the chemical but never says why anyone wanted that chemical.
whyWrong.B: It explains what a fixative does and that ambergris was scarce, but never connects either to clary sage.
whyWrong.C: It gets as far as the substitution but omits both the scarcity that created the demand and the crop itself.

tips: For a “why did X happen” goal, check that the choice contains every link from cause to outcome.

whyCorrect: The goal asks why layering works where other methods fail, so the answer must give the mechanism. Only this choice does: the shoot stays attached and keeps receiving water from the parent while it roots, so unlike a severed cutting it is never thrown onto its own reserves. That is the reason it succeeds with species that root poorly.

whyWrong.B: It gives the procedure and a drawback but never explains why the method succeeds.
whyWrong.C: It states the difference between the two methods without saying what that difference does for the plant.
whyWrong.D: It reports that difficult species are layered and describes the wounding, which is a step, not the reason it works.

commonMistakes: Describing how a technique is performed when the goal asks why it works.

whyCorrect: A balanced account has to carry both sides. This choice gives the advantage — compact notation for drug, quantity, form and timing, readable by a dispenser anywhere in Europe — and then the costs, that the patient could not read it and that similar abbreviations could be confused. The “though” is what makes it balanced rather than one-sided.

whyWrong.B: It states only what the system was and covered, with no assessment either way.
whyWrong.C: It gives two drawbacks and no advantage, so it is one-sided in the other direction.
whyWrong.D: It gives only the benefit of international legibility.

tips: For a “balanced account” goal, count the sides: the answer must contain at least one of each.

whyCorrect: “Rather than accidental” tells you the blank must mean built into the methods themselves. The passage supplies exactly that: steeping stops at equilibrium, percolation never reaches equilibrium because fresh spirit keeps arriving, so the strength difference follows from how each process works and would recur every time.

whyWrong.B: “Slight” describes the size of the difference, but the contrast is about its cause, not its magnitude.
whyWrong.C: “Temporary” would mean the difference disappears with time; equilibrium is precisely what stops steeping from catching up.
whyWrong.D: “Disputed” would put the difference in question, while the passage explains it as a settled consequence.

tips: When the frame is “X rather than accidental,” the blank names a cause that is systematic.

whyCorrect: “Not merely ineffective but” demands something worse than failing to help. The passage gives it: drying these seeds below about a quarter of their fresh weight kills them, and a store that preserves wheat for a century destroys an acorn in a fortnight. So the standard method does not just fail — it does the damage itself.

whyWrong.B: Cost is never mentioned, and expense would not be a step beyond ineffectiveness in the way the sentence requires.
whyWrong.C: Misunderstanding concerns how people regard the method, not what it does to the seed.
whyWrong.D: Difficulty of arrangement is a practical inconvenience, milder than ineffectiveness rather than worse than it.

commonMistakes: Choosing any negative word. “Not merely X but Y” requires Y to be an escalation of X.

whyCorrect: The blank describes how the care looks to an observer who does not know which drug is on the pan. Two or three grains mean nothing in a mild preparation, so to someone ignorant of the contents the elaborate precision seems out of proportion — and the passage's point is that it only seems so, because with a powerful drug those grains matter.

whyWrong.B: “Careless” is the opposite of what is described; the dispenser is working with great care.
whyWrong.C: “Habitual” says the care is routine, which is not something an outsider would find striking or worth remarking.
whyWrong.D: “Inexpensive” concerns cost, which the passage never raises.

tips: When a sentence ends “to anyone who did not know,” the blank is the mistaken impression, not the truth.

whyCorrect: The whole comparison is built on time. Sowing takes a fortnight or more, and a season for species needing a chill; the tetrazolium test answers in a few hours. The sentence then rules out accuracy as the advantage, leaving the one benefit the passage has actually demonstrated.

whyWrong.A: Nothing suggests the staining test is simpler to carry out; it involves cutting the seed and a reagent.
whyWrong.B: Certainty is ruled out by the previous sentence, which says the test does not improve on sowing for accuracy.
whyWrong.D: Cost is never compared between the two methods.

tips: When a sentence names what a method does not improve, the blank is the advantage the passage did establish.

whyCorrect: The colon after the blank supplies its definition: the delay keeps a seed shed in autumn from sprouting into a winter that would kill it. Something that prevents a fatal mistake is a protective mechanism, and “not a defect but…” signals that the blank must be a positive function.

whyWrong.A: A measurement would mean the seed is gauging something for the observer, but the clause after the colon describes protection.
whyWrong.B: A coincidence would make the timing accidental, which contradicts a mechanism that reliably prevents winter germination.
whyWrong.D: “Consequence” names the delay as a mere effect and misses the purpose the colon spells out.

tips: When a colon follows the blank, the words after it define the blank — read them first.

whyCorrect: The sentence before the underlined one establishes that the glaze could be scraped and the band repainted whenever the jar was reassigned to a different drug. The underlined sentence takes that fact and states what follows from it: the vessel was made to outlive whatever contents it happened to hold. It concludes rather than adds.

whyWrong.A: Manufacture is never discussed; the shift earlier in the passage is from decoration to the label band.
whyWrong.C: It offers no objection to collectors — the passage's remark about collectors is in the first sentence and is not disputed here.
whyWrong.D: No abbreviated Latin is quoted anywhere in the text.

tips: A final sentence that restates the preceding fact at a higher level of generality is drawing a conclusion.

whyCorrect: The text explains one operation — returning the distillation water to the still for a second pass, sometimes over fresh petals — and then names what it gains: oil that would otherwise be thrown away, and a concentrated rose water that sells on its own. Procedure plus two benefits is the whole shape of the passage.

whyWrong.B: No ranking is offered; both products are presented as gains from the same step.
whyWrong.C: No history is given; the passage describes current practice with no chronology.
whyWrong.D: No regions are named and no yields are compared.

tips: If a passage ends by listing what a practice achieves, its purpose is explanatory, not evaluative.

whyCorrect: The final clause states the value in plain terms: within their limits the rules “let a store predict the effect of a change before making it.” Because each one per cent of moisture and each five degrees roughly doubles seed life, a manager can work out what a proposed change is worth without running a decades-long trial.

whyWrong.A: The passage sets an explicit limit — below about five per cent, further drying stops helping and may harm.
whyWrong.C: Both rules are given the same doubling effect, so neither is singled out as dominant.
whyWrong.D: “Roughly doubles” is an approximation, and the text calls them rules of thumb, not a way of fixing exact years.

commonMistakes: Overstating a rule of thumb into a precise prediction. The text's own hedging words rule that out.

whyCorrect: The chemistry drives the answer: menthone converts progressively into menthol as flowering proceeds, and menthol is the cooling character buyers want. Cutting early therefore catches the oil before much of that conversion has happened. The last sentence confirms the consequence is commercial — nothing lost in weight of oil, a great deal lost in price.

whyWrong.A: Regrowth and later cuttings are never mentioned.
whyWrong.B: The conversion is described as progressive, so early oil is low in menthol rather than free of it, and nothing says it cannot be sold.
whyWrong.D: The text says explicitly that an early cut loses nothing in weight of oil.

tips: When the last sentence separates quantity from value, make sure your answer sits on the value side.

whyCorrect: The claim is that the gardener managed to a target rather than merely avoiding frost. This entry has a target in it — 62 degrees is “three degrees above what I want it” — and shows him adjusting the flue to bring the house back to that figure. A desired value plus a corrective action is exactly what managing to a target means.

whyWrong.B: Recording a hard frost and ice in the tank reports the weather and shows no intention about a temperature.
whyWrong.C: Building work and a stray ladder bear on neither temperature nor management.
whyWrong.D: Firing late because the night was bitter is frost avoidance — responding to cold, with no target named.

commonMistakes: Accepting any quotation that mentions heating. The claim needs a stated target and an adjustment toward it.

whyCorrect: The argument is that survival on the journey, not novelty, governed what he collected. This entry shows both halves at once: the primula is new and fine, which is the novelty pull, yet he takes seed only, and he gives his reason — roots would not last three months in a mule pannier. Choosing against novelty for transportability is the argument's exact shape.

whyWrong.A: Finding unnamed species establishes novelty was available but says nothing about how he decided what to take.
whyWrong.B: Hiring men and a mule is logistics with no collecting decision in it.
whyWrong.D: Ruined presses record a misfortune, not a choice made on grounds of survivability.

tips: For a claim about a decision rule, look for the entry where the collector rejects something and says why.

whyCorrect: The proposal is that the sheets can settle the question. For that to work, sheets must exist from the vanished localities, must be correctly named on re-examination, and must say where they came from. This finding supplies all three, which rules out misidentification and leaves a genuine retreat as the explanation. The other options describe the problem rather than showing the sheets can resolve it.

whyWrong.A: Recorders staying near home says something about coverage, not about whether the old records were right.
whyWrong.B: Confusability with a commoner relative is the reason the doubt exists; it does not show the sheets can settle it.
whyWrong.C: A continuing decline at the surviving sites concerns the present population and cannot address the old records.

tips: To support “evidence X can settle question Y,” the finding must show X exists and is decisive, not restate Y.

whyCorrect: The passage opens with the reason distillation fails for these flowers: the compounds carrying their scent are destroyed at the temperature it requires. Enfleurage runs cold — fat absorbing scent from living blossoms over weeks — so it captures what heat would have wrecked. That is the only thing that could justify keeping so laborious a method in use.

whyWrong.A: The flowers are renewed daily precisely because they are used at once, so storage is not what the method offers.
whyWrong.C: No comparison of quantity is made; the passage says distillation gives almost nothing, but the fault named is quality.
whyWrong.D: The text calls the method laborious, which points to more labour rather than less skilled labour.

tips: When a passage explains why the usual method fails, the blank almost always names the failure the alternative avoids.

whyCorrect: The passage names the killer in its first sentence: wet, not cold. Its model is the plant's native ground, where meltwater drains instantly away through broken rock and the neck stays dry. A bed of stone chippings with almost no soil reproduces that drainage, so the reason for an arrangement that “looks starved” is that water cannot linger around the root.

whyWrong.B: Stone chippings do not insulate, and the text has already said cold is not the main cause of death.
whyWrong.C: Mineral nutrition is never mentioned; the point of the chippings is drainage, not feeding.
whyWrong.D: Nothing in the passage concerns limiting the size of the plants.

tips: An inference blank should complete the mechanism the passage has already explained, not introduce a new benefit.

whyCorrect: “A pharmacopoeia monograph fixes what a preparation must contain and how it is to be tested for strength” and “it does not tell a dispenser when the preparation should be used” are both complete clauses. A semicolon joins two independent clauses, and it also points up the contrast between what the monograph does and does not do.

whyWrong.B: A comma with no conjunction between two independent clauses is a comma splice.
whyWrong.C: With no punctuation the clauses fuse, and “tested for strength it does not tell” reads as nonsense.
whyWrong.D: “Which” would make the second half a relative clause, but it already has its own subject “it,” so the two compete.

tips: Two clauses that state a contrast still need a real joining mark; contrast alone does not license a comma.

whyCorrect: “Each of them ready to be rounded between the palms” has no conjugated verb — it is an absolute phrase describing the state of the cut lengths. A phrase of that kind attaches to the main clause with a comma.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon requires an independent clause on both sides, and this phrase has no finite verb.
whyWrong.B: A period would leave the phrase standing alone as a sentence fragment.
whyWrong.C: “And” would signal a second clause or a second item, but what follows is a description of the lengths just mentioned.

commonMistakes: Treating “each of them ready…” as a clause. “Ready” is an adjective here, not a verb.

whyCorrect: “Safely” is an adverb sitting between the modal “can” and the verb “tolerate,” and nothing may be inserted inside that verb phrase. The blank takes no punctuation at all.

whyWrong.A: A comma cuts the adverb off from the verb it modifies and breaks “can safely tolerate” apart.
whyWrong.B: A semicolon needs a full clause on either side; “tolerate for the many hours the process takes” is not one.
whyWrong.C: A colon must follow a complete clause, and the words before it end mid verb phrase.

tips: Never punctuate between a helping verb, its adverb and the main verb.

whyCorrect: The first clause runs the whole way to “until he had passed,” and “the Society kept the register of everyone who had” is a second independent clause. A semicolon is the only offered mark able to join two independent clauses.

whyWrong.A: Without punctuation the two clauses run together and “passed the Society” misreads as a verb and object.
whyWrong.B: A coordinating conjunction joining two full clauses needs a comma in front of it; “and” alone is not enough here.
whyWrong.D: A comma with no conjunction is a splice.

tips: When a sentence already contains a long series of verbs, check whether what follows the blank has a new subject — if so, you need a clause-level mark.

whyCorrect: The clause after “so” needs a finite verb for the subject “a specimen.” “Can be matched” supplies one, and the passive is right because the specimen is what gets matched to the notebook entry rather than doing the matching.

whyWrong.A: “Can be matching” is active progressive, which makes the specimen the one doing the matching.
whyWrong.B: “Being matched” is a participle and leaves the clause without a main verb.
whyWrong.C: “To be matched” is an infinitive and likewise cannot serve as the clause's predicate.

tips: After “so that” or “so,” you need a real clause, which means a conjugated verb.

whyCorrect: The subject is “a nurseryman,” modified by the relative clause “who wants an even stand,” and the sentence still needs its main verb. “Scratches” is singular to match “nurseryman” and present to match “are” in the first half of the sentence.

whyWrong.A: “Having scratched” is a participle, so the clause after “and” would have no main verb.
whyWrong.C: “Scratching” is also a participle and leaves the same gap.
whyWrong.D: “To scratch” is an infinitive and cannot function as the predicate.

commonMistakes: Mistaking the verb inside the relative clause (“wants”) for the sentence's main verb.

whyCorrect: “Neither” used as a pronoun subject is singular — it means neither one — so the verb is “says.” The present tense also matches “is” in the two definitions before the semicolon.

whyWrong.A: “Saying” is a participle and leaves the clause after the semicolon without a finite verb, so it cannot stand as an independent clause.
whyWrong.B: “To say” is an infinitive and has the same problem.
whyWrong.D: “Say” is plural; the presence of two terms in the sentence does not make “neither” plural.

tips: “Neither,” “either” and “each” as subjects always take a singular verb.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences set out a straightforward advantage: glued specimens cannot be lifted without damage, strapped ones can be released and replaced as often as needed. The sentence after the blank reports herbaria acting on that advantage for the sheets they expect to be handled most. Practice following from a stated benefit is a result relationship.

whyWrong.B: “However” signals a contrast, but the change in practice agrees with the advantage just described.
whyWrong.C: “Beforehand” puts the change earlier in time, when it is a response to the comparison.
whyWrong.D: “Admittedly” concedes a point against the argument, and nothing here works against it.

tips: Advantage stated, then people adopting it, means a result transition.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences establish the order of arrival: light terpenes boil low and come first, the heavier odour-bearing compounds boil higher and arrive later in the run. If you collect only the beginning, you have the terpenes and not the character. The last sentence is that deduction, so the transition marks a consequence.

whyWrong.A: “Nevertheless” signals a contrast, but the thin smell follows directly from the boiling order.
whyWrong.B: “By contrast” needs two things set against each other, and the last sentence draws a conclusion from both preceding ones.
whyWrong.C: “For instance” would make the thin distillate an example of the compounds' boiling points rather than their effect.

tips: When the last sentence applies the preceding facts to a practical case, it is a consequence.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives what alphabetical order does for someone with no botany; the second gives what classified order does for a worker comparing relatives. The sentence after the blank condenses both into one line — one arrangement serves the visitor, the other the specialist. That is a summary, so the transition must mark one.

whyWrong.A: “Afterwards” marks time, and nothing here happens in sequence.
whyWrong.C: “Even so” concedes against what came before, but the final sentence agrees with both earlier sentences.
whyWrong.D: “For instance” would introduce a specific case, whereas the last sentence is more general than what precedes it.

tips: A closing sentence that pairs off two earlier points one-for-one is a summary.

whyCorrect: The goal is why the data must be taken in the field, so the answer needs the irreversibility plus the consequence of losing it. This choice has both: the data cannot be recovered once the collector has left, and without exact place, altitude and habitat a lot cannot be matched to a reintroduction site — which matters because valleys differ in cold tolerance. Nothing else in the notes explains the urgency of the moment of collection.

whyWrong.A: It gives the consequence of missing data but never says why the record has to be made at the site.
whyWrong.B: It states what is recorded and when, without saying what is lost if the recording is skipped.
whyWrong.D: It contrasts old and new practice but supplies no reason the field is the only opportunity.

tips: A goal containing “must” usually needs the choice that says what becomes impossible otherwise.

whyCorrect: The goal asks why, so the answer must give the mechanism, not just the pattern. This choice does: the extra petals of a double flower stand in place of the parts that make pollen and nectar, so there is nothing for an insect to collect — and the four-times-higher bee count on single-flowered beds, which keep both, confirms it.

whyWrong.A: It states the outcome and what gardeners do about it without explaining the cause.
whyWrong.B: It puts the two facts side by side but never says the petals replace the nectar-bearing parts, which is the whole explanation.
whyWrong.D: It gives the survey result and gardeners' response, with no reason for the difference.

commonMistakes: Offering the evidence for a pattern when the goal asks for the cause of it.

whyCorrect: To show a cost turned into something useful, the answer has to name the cost and then the uses. This choice sets the alternative — paying a contractor to remove a bulky wet material with no oil left in it — against both practical uses in the notes: lavender stalks dried and burnt as fuel under the boiler, rose petals ploughed back into the fields.

whyWrong.A: It gives only the cost side, with no use found for the material.
whyWrong.C: It defines the spent charge and its awkwardness, stopping before either the cost or the uses.
whyWrong.D: It lists the two uses but never mentions the disposal cost they replace, so no transformation is shown.

tips: “Turns a cost into a use” needs both halves in the sentence, or the contrast disappears.

whyCorrect: The sentence before the blank is doing all the work: “Nothing is opened and nothing is broken.” Candling judges the air cell through the shell by lamplight, so the egg it has just assessed can still be sold. The blank must name that undamaged state.

whyWrong.A: Sorting is what the grader does with the information afterwards; it is not the condition the egg is left in.
whyWrong.B: No weighing is described — the gauge reads the depth of the air cell, not mass.
whyWrong.D: Chilling is never mentioned; the room is dark, not cold.

tips: When a sentence says “valued precisely because it leaves X…,” look for the property the preceding sentence has just asserted.

whyCorrect: The bloom dries into a film across thousands of pores, and the passage says what happens once it is scrubbed away: the egg loses water faster and lets in bacteria the film had blocked. A layer that closes pores against water loss and microbes is a seal.

whyWrong.A: Colour is never mentioned; the film is described as thin and moist, not pigmented.
whyWrong.B: “Cushions” suggests protection against impact, but the harms described are evaporation and infection.
whyWrong.D: “Hardens” would be about shell strength, which the passage never raises.

commonMistakes: Choosing a generic protective word. The specific harms named — water out, bacteria in — identify the mechanism as sealing.

whyCorrect: Read the phrase in place: broodiness is a nuisance or an asset according to what the flock is kept for — that is, according to the purpose for which it is raised and looked after. The passage has just contrasted a keeper who wants eggs with one who wants chicks, so “kept” refers to keeping livestock, which is maintaining them.

whyWrong.A: “Withheld” means held back from someone, which makes no sense of a flock raised for a purpose.
whyWrong.B: “Postponed” applies to events in time, not to animals.
whyWrong.D: “Detained” means held against departure, and the sentence is about the purpose of keeping the birds, not about confinement.

tips: Substitute each choice into the sentence in full. Only one leaves the sentence saying what the passage has just argued.

whyCorrect: The contrast in the last sentence is that the fisherman builds no trap around the river — the river is the trap. The buck sits in a gap so the whole flow must pass through it, and eels carried in cannot turn back against the current. So the current itself becomes the thing there is no escaping.

whyWrong.B: Nothing is measured; the funnel catches eels rather than gauging flow.
whyWrong.C: The buck does not slow the water, and a gentler current would let eels turn and swim out.
whyWrong.D: Season is not the point; the passage describes eels moving downstream at night, not a yearly cycle.

tips: The last sentence's “he simply makes the river's own movement…” means the blank must describe the current, not the trap.

whyCorrect: The problem stated at the start is that a bird with a broken flight feather cannot just be rested, because the next moult — when a new feather would grow — may be ten months away. Imping splices a saved feather onto the broken shaft, so the wing is usable immediately. The blank names what the falconer no longer has to wait for.

whyWrong.A: Manning is taming a hawk to human company and has nothing to do with the feather.
whyWrong.B: Weight is a condition falconers manage, but no weight problem is described here.
whyWrong.C: Rehooding is a handling step, unrelated to the ten-month wait the passage sets up.

tips: An “X without waiting for Y” blank names the slow process the passage has already identified.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives the principle: ducks will not approach a person but will follow a fox. The rest describes how a small reddish dog exploits that — showing itself in gap after gap so the mobbing birds draw themselves further up the curve of the pipe, with the decoyman staying hidden until they cannot turn. The purpose is to explain how a defensive instinct is converted into a way of leading birds.

whyWrong.A: Decoy ducks are never mentioned, so no comparison is made.
whyWrong.B: Only “a small reddish dog” is mentioned; no breeds and no history are given.
whyWrong.C: The birds' wariness is the starting fact the method exploits, not the point of the passage.

tips: When a text opens with an animal's instinct and then describes a technique, its purpose is usually to show how the instinct is used.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives a difference anyone can see: thick white stands up in a fresh egg and spreads in a stale one. The underlined sentence reports the move that made it measurable — Haugh's micrometer reading of the white's height, corrected for the egg's weight. The sentences after it explain the correction and note that graders still use the figure, which only makes sense once a number exists.

whyWrong.A: That explanation is given in the next sentence, which justifies the correction; the underlined sentence only states that the correction was applied.
whyWrong.B: Grader preference is not discussed; the sentence is about measurement, not about which eggs are wanted.
whyWrong.C: No disagreement appears anywhere in the passage.

tips: When a passage moves from “you can see it” to “graders use the figure,” the sentence in between is the one that made it a number.

whyCorrect: The passage makes two moves. It reports the healing belief and says flatly that no experiment has ever supported it. Then it supplies the tench's real distinguishing trait — surviving water so poor in oxygen that carp gasp and pike die — which is why the fish turns up in the muddiest ponds where other fish fail. The final sentence draws both together: the reputation records where the fish was found, not what it did.

whyWrong.A: The causation is reversed; tench were stocked in muddy ponds because they could live there.
whyWrong.B: The text says no experiment ever supported the belief and that it survived in print for three centuries, so testing did not end it.
whyWrong.D: The passage denies any demonstrated healing effect.

tips: When a text ends by re-explaining a belief's origin, the main idea has to include both the debunking and the explanation.

whyCorrect: The second sentence names the constraint: the message travels in a light tube on the bird's leg, and “its weight sets the limit on what can be sent.” Photographing despatches down to a film a few centimetres square packs thousands of messages into that same tiny weight, so the limitation photography answers is carrying capacity.

whyWrong.A: Homing is never in question; the passage assumes the birds return.
whyWrong.B: Interception and secrecy are not mentioned, and film is not described as a security measure.
whyWrong.C: Rain damage never appears in the text.

commonMistakes: Assuming photography was for secrecy. The passage states the constraint explicitly, and it is weight.

whyCorrect: The scientist's objection is that elver numbers rose everywhere that year, so the rise above the weir might have nothing to do with the pass. To answer it the engineers need a comparison with rivers that had no pass. A rise far larger than at unaltered weirs over the same two years leaves a difference the coast-wide surge cannot explain, and that surplus is what the pass would account for.

whyWrong.A: An undamaged pass shows the structure survived, not that elvers used it.
whyWrong.C: A rise below the weir is exactly what the coast-wide increase predicts, so it supports the objection rather than the claim.
whyWrong.D: A coast-wide rise above the previous decade is the scientist's point stated over again.

tips: When a rival explanation is regional, the winning evidence is a control — a comparable site without the intervention.

whyCorrect: Anandan's claim is about relative priority, so the useful entry is one where manure and meat are both valued and can be compared. This one is: eleven loads carted from under the cote fetch 3s. 8d. while the season's squabs fetch 2s. 1d. The manure is worth more, and it is entered first, which is precisely the reversal she describes.

whyWrong.A: The licence establishes the lord's right to keep a dovecote and values nothing.
whyWrong.C: A new door with ironwork is a maintenance cost and shows no product at all.
whyWrong.D: The posts and thatch describe construction, which bears on neither manure nor meat.

commonMistakes: Choosing an entry that mentions the dovecote rather than one that lets the two products be weighed against each other.

whyCorrect: The conclusion has two parts, so the data must show both. Lay rises from 2.6 at 10 hours to 5.4 at 14 hours, a gain of 2.8 eggs per hen per week; from 14 to 16 hours it rises only from 5.4 to 5.6, a gain of 0.2. Longer days raise the rate, and the last two-hour step buys almost nothing — exactly the student's claim.

whyWrong.A: The highest figure alone shows the direction of the effect but nothing about diminishing gains.
whyWrong.B: The lowest figure likewise establishes only one end of the range.
whyWrong.D: This is false on the numbers: the steps are +1.3, +1.5 and +0.2, so the increase is not steady.

tips: For a “gains taper off” conclusion, compute the differences between consecutive rows before choosing.

whyCorrect: The comparison is the evidence. Where the cote stands against a rat-infested yard the lowest nests start a metre up, the wall below is rendered smooth and a projecting stone course juts out; where the cote stands free on a staddle, out of a rat's reach already, holes run right down. A smooth band with an overhang is a barrier to anything climbing, and it is present only where climbing animals are a threat.

whyWrong.A: No structural need is mentioned, and a smooth render with a projecting course is not a strengthening detail.
whyWrong.B: A potence swings inside the cote; nothing about it would require the outer wall to be rendered smooth or the lowest nests to be raised.
whyWrong.D: Sweeping does not explain the projecting stone course or why free-standing cotes have holes all the way down.

tips: When a text contrasts two versions of the same structure, the feature present in only one is explained by the condition present in only one.

whyCorrect: The second sentence is the test that settles it. If a pigeon worked out its heading by remembering the twists of the outward journey, then scrambling that journey — a deliberately circuitous route with the basket rotated the whole way — would wreck the heading. It does not; the birds set off just as consistently. So route memory cannot be what the initial choice depends on.

whyWrong.A: The first sentence already rules this out by using sites the birds have never seen, so it is not what the second experiment tests.
whyWrong.C: Nothing in either experiment removes the birds' sight of the ground; they are released in the open and watched.
whyWrong.D: Distance is never varied in the experiments described, so no conclusion about it follows.

tips: An inference from an experiment names the variable the experiment removed — here, knowledge of the outward path.

whyCorrect: “Which is the only part of the bed still holding water” is a non-restrictive relative clause: it adds information about the sump rather than picking out which sump is meant. A non-restrictive clause is set off with a comma.

whyWrong.A: With no comma the clause reads as restrictive, implying there are several outlets and this identifies one.
whyWrong.B: A semicolon needs an independent clause after it, and a “which” clause is dependent.
whyWrong.C: A colon must follow a complete clause and introduce a list or explanation; a relative clause is neither.

tips: A “which” clause adding extra detail takes a comma; a “that” clause identifying which one takes none.

whyCorrect: “Rather than mounted on it” completes the last clause of the passage, and nothing follows. A sentence needs terminal punctuation, so the full stop is the only workable choice.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon promises a second independent clause, and there is nothing after it.
whyWrong.C: Leaving the sentence unpunctuated gives no end to it at all.
whyWrong.D: A comma also leaves the sentence hanging, promising a continuation that never comes.

commonMistakes: Forgetting that the blank can be the end of the passage. Check whether anything follows before assuming a join is needed.

whyCorrect: “Each fancier's clock is sealed before the race by an official of the club” and “this is what makes the recorded times comparable at all” are both complete clauses with their own subjects and verbs. A semicolon joins two independent clauses and keeps the comment attached to the practice it explains.

whyWrong.B: A comma with no conjunction between independent clauses is a splice.
whyWrong.C: With no punctuation the clauses fuse into a run-on.
whyWrong.D: “Which” after a colon leaves a fragment, since “which this is…” has no main clause to attach to and the second half already has the subject “this.”

tips: A second clause beginning with “this is” is nearly always independent — it needs a semicolon or a period.

whyCorrect: “Dropping onto the board inside and finding no way out again” is a participial phrase describing the racer as it comes through the wires. It has no subject or finite verb of its own, so it attaches to the main clause with a comma.

whyWrong.A: A colon introduces a list or an explanation after a complete clause; a trailing participial phrase is neither.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon requires an independent clause on each side, and a participial phrase is not one.
whyWrong.D: With no punctuation, “drives through the wires dropping” runs the action and the modifier together and obscures which is the main verb.

tips: An -ing phrase tacked onto the end of a clause is set off with a comma.

whyCorrect: “Flock” is a collective noun, and the passage treats it as a single unit — the previous sentence says the flock is managed as a unit and individual birds are not tracked. A collective taken as one body takes a singular verb, and the present tense matches the general description of how such a flock is run.

whyWrong.A: “Are” is plural, which would treat the flock as a set of individuals — the reading the previous sentence rules out.
whyWrong.B: “Have been” is plural and shifts to the present perfect, describing a completed event rather than standard practice.
whyWrong.C: “Were being” is past progressive and turns a general policy into something that happened on one occasion.

tips: Let the surrounding sentence tell you whether a collective noun is being treated as one thing or many.

whyCorrect: “Since the first counts were made in the 1970s” marks a stretch of time running from the past up to now, which calls for the present perfect. The subject is “numbers,” plural, so the form is “have fallen” — and it matches “has been cut” in the second half of the sentence.

whyWrong.B: The simple past “fell” describes a finished event and does not fit a decline continuing to the present.
whyWrong.C: “Falls” is singular and present simple, wrong in both number and time frame.
whyWrong.D: The past perfect “had fallen” needs a later past reference point, and none is given.

tips: “Since” plus a past starting point is the standard signal for the present perfect.

whyCorrect: The bells belong to more than one falconer — the sentence describes a large meet with the sound carrying across the whole field and one bird's pair distinguishable from another's. The possessive of the plural “falconers” is formed with an apostrophe after the s.

whyWrong.B: “Falconer's” is singular possessive, which would mean one falconer, leaving nothing for the bells to be told apart from.
whyWrong.C: “Falconers” with no apostrophe is a plain plural and cannot show possession of the bells.
whyWrong.D: “Falconers's” is not a form English uses for a plural already ending in s.

tips: Work out the number of owners from the situation described, then place the apostrophe.

whyCorrect: The sentence before the blank reports the regulation as the solution to small-mesh traps. The sentence after says the rule is easier to write than to enforce, because a legal net can be fished with an illegal liner. That undercuts the solution just described, so the transition must be contrastive.

whyWrong.B: “Therefore” would make the enforcement problem a consequence of the rule's existence rather than a difficulty with it.
whyWrong.C: “Similarly” claims a parallel, but the second sentence works against the first.
whyWrong.D: “In addition” presents it as another supporting point when it is an objection.

tips: A sentence naming a loophole in the measure just described always needs a contrast transition.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences establish that dovecote floors were a source of saltpetre for gunpowder. The sentence after the blank reports commissioners holding the right to enter and dig those floors regardless of the owner's wishes — a power that follows directly from the material's military value. The transition therefore marks a consequence.

whyWrong.A: “In particular” would narrow the previous point to a special case, but a legal right of entry is a different kind of statement.
whyWrong.C: “By contrast” needs opposition, and the last sentence follows from what precedes it.
whyWrong.D: “Meanwhile” marks a parallel event in time, which is not the relationship here.

tips: A legal power granted because of a resource's value is an effect, so use a result word.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences describe a protective membrane sweeping across the eye throughout the stoop. That raises an obvious problem — a bird that covers its eyes cannot see its quarry — and the last sentence resolves it: the membrane is largely transparent. An emphasis transition marks that this detail is what makes the whole arrangement work.

whyWrong.A: “In contrast” would set the transparency against the protection, but the two work together.
whyWrong.B: “Afterwards” puts the transparency later in time, whereas it holds during the dive.
whyWrong.D: “Otherwise” means “if that were not so,” which does not fit a sentence stating what is in fact the case.

tips: When the final sentence removes an objection the reader was about to raise, an emphasis word such as “crucially” fits.

whyCorrect: The goal is how the meaning changed, so the answer must show a before and an after. This choice does: the word entered English naming the pond itself and had by 1800 extended to the wooden birds, which the seventeenth century had called stales. Two senses and a direction of movement between them.

whyWrong.B: It gives the older word for the birds but records no change in what “decoy” meant.
whyWrong.C: It gives the word's origin, which is where it came from rather than how its sense shifted afterwards.
whyWrong.D: It dates the first ponds, which is a fact about the structures and not about the word.

tips: A “how did the meaning change” goal needs both the earlier sense and the later one in the same sentence.

whyCorrect: The goal asks why the fixed-date method was abandoned, so the answer needs the flaw and the replacement. This choice has both: the passage shifts by up to three weeks with the weather, so a single fixed date can miss it entirely, and the site now counts on five dates across six weeks and takes the highest.

whyWrong.B: It describes the current practice without saying what was wrong with the old one.
whyWrong.C: It gives the variability but never connects it to the failure of a fixed date or to the new method.
whyWrong.D: It states that the passage is brief, which is background rather than a reason for changing practice.

commonMistakes: Choosing the note that states the problem alone. A “why no longer” goal needs the problem and the response.

whyCorrect: The claim has two halves: the phrases survive, and the practice behind them does not. This choice carries both — expressions from sixteenth-century falconry still in general use, with few speakers aware of the origin. Naming two of the phrases makes it an illustration rather than a bare assertion.

whyWrong.A: It explains one falconry term but never says the phrase outlived the practice.
whyWrong.C: Same problem: it gives an original meaning with no statement that the expression survives in ordinary use.
whyWrong.D: It dates the phrases' entry into English but says nothing about their survival or the loss of their original context.

tips: To illustrate a claim, the choice must contain a concrete case and the point the case is meant to prove.
